summary_html: Agency decides to **remove a child immediately** due to **imminent danger** prior to a court order. Federal law (ASFA/IV-E) requires later **court findings** on reasonable efforts; constitutional limits (due process; search/seizure) apply. In Alabama the age of majority is 19 (Ala. Code § 26-1-1), and for child abuse and neglect reporting a "child" is a person under 18, or a person under 19 who is in need of protective services and does not qualify for adult protective services (Ala. Code § 26-14-1(3)). If a report is marked **indicated**, the full § 26-14-7.1 hearing (counsel, witnesses, cross-examination, subpoenas, an impartial hearing officer) is available only to a person connected with a facility, agency, or home that cares for and controls children; everyone else, including a parent investigated at home, receives the DHR administrative record review, which DHR describes as "provided for those persons not entitled to a hearing" and for which the DHR review page states no deadline (dhr.alabama.gov/child-protective-services/child-abuse-neglect-administrative-reviews).

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit
key_cases.holding: The Eleventh Circuit held that due process permits a warrantless emergency removal where the totality of the circumstances shows objectively imminent danger to the child, rejecting the Second Circuit's rule that the availability of time to obtain a court order alone defeats the emergency exception.
key_cases.relevance: It is the controlling authority in Alabama's circuit on when an emergency removal decision is constitutionally justified.
key_cases.quote: We agree that the sole focus should not be whether there is time to obtain a court order.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The plurality held that Washington's breathtakingly broad nonparental visitation statute was unconstitutional as applied because the court gave no special weight to a fit parent's determination of her children's best interests.
key_cases.relevance: An emergency removal must rest on more than a judgment that the State could make a better decision than the parent.
key_cases.quote: there is a presumption that fit parents act in the best interests of their children

key_cases.case_name: N.G. v. Blount County Department of Human Resources
key_cases.court: Court of Civil Appeals of Alabama
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed dependency findings based on the mother's medication abuse and domestic violence and held that an indigent parent has no constitutional right to appointed counsel in a dependency proceeding, although Ala. Code 12-15-308(c) obliges the juvenile court to advise a parent of the right to counsel at the 72-hour shelter-care hearing and to investigate indigency.
key_cases.relevance: The case reviews a pickup order followed by a shelter-care hearing and shelter-care order maintaining DHR custody.
key_cases.quote: an indigent parent does not have a constitutional right to the appointment of an attorney in a dependency proceeding

key_cases.holding: The Court denied State-agent immunity to the CA/N investigator, who never made the home visit required by Ala. Admin. Code r. 660-5-34-.05(1)(b), and to the ongoing worker, who ignored her supervisor's binding written instructions, but granted immunity to the two supervisors whose duties involved judgment.
key_cases.relevance: The child was released to the mother's custody without the required home visit and later died.
key_cases.quote: because Watson has not submitted substantial evidence indicating that she complied with subsection (b), Watson has not demonstrated that she is entitled to State-agent immunity

key_cases.court: United States District Court for the Middle District of Alabama
key_cases.holding: A three-judge court held Alabama's summary child-removal statute unconstitutional, ruling that removing a child from a parent without prior notice and a hearing violates procedural due process absent immediate or threatened harm, that a post-seizure hearing must follow as soon as practicable, and that the statute's welfare and neglect standards were unconstitutionally vague.
key_cases.relevance: The court found no emergency where the child was clothed, clean and unharmed and the home was clean and stocked with food, which is the factual benchmark for an unjustified emergency removal in Alabama.
key_cases.quote: this Court is of the opinion that Alabama Code Title 13, § 352(4) violates the procedural due process clause of the Fourteenth Amendment
